lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: A class is a blueprint and an object is one thing built from it.

blocks.md:
## The idea

A class is a blueprint and an object is one thing built from it. `__init__` runs when the object is created and stores its data on `self`. A method is a function that lives on the class and receives the object as `self`. A child class written as `class Cat(Animal)` inherits every method of its parent and may replace any of them; `super()` reaches the parent's version.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: A child class defines its own `__init__` and never calls `super().__init__()`. What happens to the parent's constructor?
options: Python raises an error at once
blocks.why: Defining `__init__` in the child replaces the parent's. The parent's version runs only when you call it through `super()`.

blocks.q: Write a class `Counter` whose constructor takes an optional `start` (default 0). `inc()` adds 1 and returns the new value; `reset()` sets the value to 0 and returns 0. Keep the value in `self.value`.
blocks.test:
c = Counter()
print(c.inc())
print(c.inc())
print(c.reset())
print(Counter(5).inc())

cards.a: The object the method was called on.
Cat inherits from Animal.
When a new object is created.

lessons.title: Lists and loops
lessons.summary: A list keeps values in order.

blocks.md:
## The idea

A list keeps values in order. You read one with an index that starts at 0, add with `append`, and walk through all of them with `for`. A slice `xs[1:3]` copies part of a list. A list comprehension builds a new list in one line from an old one.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

## A worked example

```python
xs = [3, 1, 4]
xs.append(1)
squares = [x * x for x in xs]
print(squares, len(xs))
```

Change one line and predict the new output before you run it again. The mistake people make most often here is running first and reading second.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
xs = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(xs[1:3], xs[-1])
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: What does `xs[0]` return for `xs = [7, 8, 9]`?
blocks.why: Indexes start at 0, so the first item is `xs[0]`.

cards.a: At 0.
Adds one item to the end of the list.
The last item.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.summary: A dictionary maps keys to values.

blocks.md:
## The idea

A dictionary maps keys to values. You read with `d[key]`, which fails for a missing key, or with `d.get(key, default)`, which does not. `for k, v in d.items()` walks through pairs. Keys must be values that cannot change, such as strings and numbers.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

## A worked example

```python
ages = {'ana': 31, 'ben': 27}
ages['cy'] = 40
for name, age in ages.items():
    print(name, age)
```

Change one line and predict the new output before you run it again. The mistake people make most often here is running first and reading second.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
d = {'a': 1}
print(d.get('b', 0) + d['a'])
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: Which of these can be a dictionary key?
blocks.why: Keys must be hashable. Strings are; lists, dictionaries and sets are not.

cards.q: How do you read a key that may be missing?
cards.a: `d.get(key, default)`.
Pairs of key and value.

cards.q: Can a list be a key?
cards.a: No, keys must be hashable.

lessons.title: Functions and arguments
lessons.summary: A function names a piece of work.

blocks.md:
## The idea

A function names a piece of work. Arguments go in, `return` hands one value back, and a function without `return` gives `None`. A default value such as `def greet(name, loud=False)` makes an argument optional. Names created inside a function stay inside it.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

## A worked example

```python
def area(w, h=1):
    return w * h

print(area(3), area(3, 2))
```

Change one line and predict the new output before you run it again. The mistake people make most often here is running first and reading second.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
def f(x):
    x = x + 1

print(f(1))
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: What does a function return when it has no `return` statement?
blocks.why: Without `return`, the call evaluates to `None`.

cards.a: Ends the function and hands a value back.
A value used when the caller leaves the argument out.

cards.q: What does a function with no return give?
cards.a: `None`.

lessons.title: Strings and formatting
lessons.summary: A string is text, and it cannot be changed in place: every method returns a new string.

blocks.md:
## The idea

A string is text, and it cannot be changed in place: every method returns a new string. `split` cuts text into a list, `join` glues a list back, and `strip` removes spaces at both ends. An f-string such as `f'{x:.2f}'` puts a value into text with a format.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

## A worked example

```python
line = ' a,b,c '
parts = line.strip().split(',')
print('-'.join(parts), f'{3.14159:.2f}')
```

Change one line and predict the new output before you run it again. The mistake people make most often here is running first and reading second.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
s = 'abc'
s.upper()
print(s)
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: What does `' hi '.strip()` return?
blocks.why: `strip` removes whitespace from both ends and returns a new string.

cards.q: Can a string be changed in place?
cards.a: No. Methods return a new string.
A list of the pieces between commas.

cards.q: What does `:.2f` do in an f-string?
cards.a: Formats a number with two decimals.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files
lessons.summary: `open(path)` gives a file object, and `with` closes it for you even when an error happens.

blocks.md:
## The idea

`open(path)` gives a file object, and `with` closes it for you even when an error happens. Reading gives text; iterating gives one line at a time, each ending in a newline. Mode `'w'` replaces the file and `'a'` adds to its end.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

## A worked example

```python
with open('notes.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('one\ntwo\n')
with open('notes.txt') as f:
    print([line.strip() for line in f])
```

Change one line and predict the new output before you run it again. The mistake people make most often here is running first and reading second.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
print(len('one\ntwo\n'.splitlines()))
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: What does opening a file with mode `'w'` do to its old contents?
options: Keeps them and adds to the end
blocks.why: `'w'` truncates the file. Use `'a'` to add to the end.

cards.a: The file is closed for you, even after an error.

cards.q: Which mode adds to the end?
What does each line end with when you iterate a file?
cards.a: A newline.

lessons.title: Errors and exceptions
lessons.summary: An exception stops the program where the problem happens.

blocks.md:
## The idea

An exception stops the program where the problem happens. `try` runs code that may fail and `except SomeError` handles that one kind of failure. Catch the narrowest error you can, so real bugs are not hidden. `raise ValueError('why')` signals a problem of your own.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
try:
    print(1 / 0)
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print('no')
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: Why is a bare `except:` usually a mistake?
options: It hides every error, including real bugs
blocks.why: A bare except swallows everything, so mistakes you did not expect disappear silently.

cards.a: Signals an error on purpose.
The narrowest kind you know how to handle.

cards.q: What happens to an uncaught exception?
cards.a: The program stops with a traceback.

lessons.title: Modules and imports
lessons.summary: A module is a file of Python you can reuse.

blocks.md:
## The idea

A module is a file of Python you can reuse. `import math` gives you `math.sqrt`; `from math import sqrt` gives the name directly. The standard library covers dates, paths, random numbers and much more. Your own file `tools.py` is imported as `import tools`.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

## A worked example

```python
import math
from statistics import mean
print(math.sqrt(16), mean([1, 2, 3]))
```

Change one line and predict the new output before you run it again. The mistake people make most often here is running first and reading second.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
import math
print(math.floor(2.7) + math.ceil(2.1))
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: After `import math`, how do you call the square root function?
blocks.why: A plain import keeps names inside the module, so you write `math.sqrt`.

cards.a: A file of Python code you can import.

cards.q: What does `from m import f` do?
cards.a: Brings the name `f` in directly.

cards.q: How do you import your own `tools.py`?
cards.a: `import tools`.

lessons.title: Testing your code
lessons.summary: A test is code that checks other code.

blocks.md:
## The idea

A test is code that checks other code. `assert expr` stops with an error when `expr` is false. Write a test for the normal case, for an edge such as an empty list, and for an input that should fail. A test that never failed has not proved anything yet: break the code once to see it fail.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

## A worked example

```python
def total(xs):
    return sum(xs)

assert total([1, 2]) == 3
assert total([]) == 0
print('ok')
```

Change one line and predict the new output before you run it again. The mistake people make most often here is running first and reading second.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
def double(x):
    return x * 2

print(double(2) == 4, double('a') == 'aa')
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: What does `assert x > 0` do when `x` is -1?
blocks.why: A false assertion raises `AssertionError` and stops the program there.

cards.a: An unusual input such as an empty list or zero.
Stops with an error when its condition is false.
To see that the test can fail.

lessons.title: Putting a small program together
lessons.summary: A program is small parts that each do one thing: read input, turn it into data, compute, and print.

blocks.md:
## The idea

A program is small parts that each do one thing: read input, turn it into data, compute, and print. Keep the computing part in functions that take values and return values, so they can be tested without files or a keyboard. Put the part that runs everything under `if __name__ == '__main__':`.

Read it once, then read the example below line by line and say out loud what each line does before you run it. Saying it first is what makes the next questions easy.

blocks.q:
What does this print?
```python
def parse(line):
    a, b = line.split(',')
    return int(a) + int(b)

print(parse('2,3'))
```
blocks.why: Trace it one line at a time with the rule from the lesson.

blocks.q: Why keep computing code in functions that take and return values?
options: They can be tested without files or input
blocks.why: A function that depends only on its arguments can be checked with a one-line test.

cards.a: The code that runs the program.

cards.q: What makes a function easy to test?
cards.a: It takes values and returns values.

cards.q: What are the four parts of a small program?
cards.a: Read, turn into data, compute, print.

drills.title: Animal and Dog classes
drills.prompt: From memory, write a class `Animal` with `__init__(self, name)` and a method `speak(self)` that returns `name + ' makes a sound'`. Then write `Dog(Animal)` that overrides `speak` to return `name + ' says woof'`.
hints: Overriding means defining a method with the same name in the child.

drills.title: Squares of the even numbers
drills.prompt: From memory, write `even_squares(xs)` that returns a list with the square of every even number in `xs`, in order.
drills.solution:
def even_squares(xs):
    return [x * x for x in xs if x % 2 == 0]

drills.title: Count the words
drills.prompt: From memory, write `count_words(text)` that returns a dictionary from each word (split on spaces) to how many times it appears.

drills.title: Explain try and except
drills.prompt: Without looking, explain what `try` and `except` do and why a bare `except:` is a mistake.
drills.solution: try runs code that may fail; except handles one named kind of failure. A bare except hides every error, including bugs you did not expect.

Write `count_words(text)` so it returns a dictionary from each word to how often it appears. **Use this name** so the checks can call it.
